Project background and objective Planned production volume could not remain dependent on one can supplier, so an alternative source had to be qualified. The candidate can differed from the incumbent in alloy ratio, bottom thickness, dimensional tolerance, burrs, and surface condition. Even when component dimensions were within tolerance, those differences could affect beading and crimping geometry, sealing, can-cap laser welding, and vent safety.
As the lead process-validation engineer, I connected drawing and certificate review, incoming-inspection criteria, reset of the existing assembly conditions, sample-cell builds, sectioning and teardown, internal quality and safety tests, and cell-performance evaluation. Purchasing owned supplier, quotation, and order changes; quality owned incoming and outgoing disposition plus the official report; cell engineering owned formation, capacity, and life evaluation; production supported lot-level sample builds.
The objective was to move beyond component inspection and verify the alternative can through actual cell processing and safety performance, establishing both the usable line conditions and the basis for a pilot supply transition.
Supplier-change validationConnect incoming inspection to official transport-safety testing through one change-control flowDrawings, certificates, and actual measurements were linked to process conditions, cell quality/performance, three 200-cell lots, and official UN38.3.01CHANGEAlloy·thickness·tolerance·burr comparison02IQCMeasurement points·appearance criteria03PROCESSBeading·crimping·laser reset04CELLQuality·safety·performance05PILOT200 cells × 3 lots06TRANSITIONUN38.3·purchase-order changeSupplier-change validation flow Component change Potentially affected process Primary check Alloy and bottom thickness Beading, crimping, and vent Geometry, press conditions, burst pressure Dimensions and tolerances Beading and crimping/sizing Total height, inner diameter, sealing, and airtightness Burrs and surface condition Incoming, assembly, and appearance inspection Measurement points, limit samples, and assembly damage Can-cap contact condition Laser welding Weld appearance, cross-section, and teardown result Cell-level effect of the change Formation, performance, and safety Capacity, life, compression/drop, and UN38.3 The change was checked in the order of incoming quality, process conditions, cell safety, and performance. No single stage was treated as sufficient on its own; the same component changes had to remain acceptable through the next process and test.
1. [Material·Measurement] Component comparison and IQC criteria Compare incumbent and candidate parts Drawings and material certificates were cross-checked, followed by actual measurement of the bottom and wall sections, dimensional tolerances, burrs, scratches, and surface condition. Measurement points and appearance disposition were fixed so that the incumbent and candidate parts were compared under one basis.
The differences found at incoming inspection were linked to the next process instead of ending as component pass/fail decisions. Bottom thickness and alloy were tied to beading, crimping, and vent behavior; dimensional tolerance to total height, inner diameter, and sealing; burr and surface condition to assembly damage and appearance checks.
Incoming-inspection gate Cross-check drawings, certificates, and actual measurements Repeat bottom and wall measurements at fixed locations Compare burrs, scratches, and surface condition with limit samples Assign each change to affected processes and downstream checks Release only accepted candidate parts into sample-cell builds The results were transferred into IQC criteria, the part specification, the change-review sheet, and limit samples. Incoming inspection served as the first gate into cell-level process validation rather than the final supplier decision.
2. [Machine·Method] Existing-equipment processability and condition reset Beading and crimping/sizing Different can thickness and tolerance could change beading geometry, crimping pressure, total height, inner diameter, and sealing even under the incumbent settings. Beading-knife height, depth, and pressure, along with crimping/sizing pressure and height conditions, were rechecked for the candidate can.
Conditions were not changed all at once. Process-specific samples compared beading shape, total height, inner diameter, crimp appearance, and airtightness. The selected conditions were then checked under the same positions and criteria during the lot trials so that the same setting could be used across operators and lots.
Can-cap laser welding Changes in can-cap contact condition and gap could alter the joint under the same laser settings. Candidate-can weld samples were evaluated through appearance, sectioning, and cell teardown.
Component difference, equipment alignment, and laser condition were separated before the applicable condition was selected from the actual joint result. Weld disposition was connected with beading/crimping geometry, sealing, and downstream cell tests rather than treated as an isolated result.
Field application The confirmed beading, crimping/sizing, and laser conditions were transferred into the process-condition sheet and sample-evaluation record. Manufacturing used one setting sequence for each lot, while engineering and quality applied the same height, sealing, and weld criteria.
3. [Measurement] Cell quality, safety, and performance validation The can is both the external shell and part of the sealing and pressure-relief system. Correct assembly geometry was insufficient if leakage, vent behavior, transport safety, or cell performance changed.
Internal quality and safety tests Assembly appearance, total height, inner diameter, airtightness, and leakage Top and bottom compression Drop testing Vent burst-pressure check Weld sectioning and cell teardown After the internal geometry, sealing, and pressure-relief checks, official-test samples were built. Quality reviewed the test results and official report, while engineering linked them to the assembly route and sample history.
Cell performance and official UN38.3 Cell engineering checked formation, capacity, and life for the alternative-can condition. The condition meeting the process, safety, and performance criteria proceeded to the official UN38.3 transport-safety test and passed.
This connected component inspection, processability, internal safety tests, and official transport safety in one change-control sequence.
4. 600-cell / three-lot pilot validation and supply transition The selected conditions were used to produce 200 cells per lot across three lots, 600 cells in total. Each lot used the same criteria for assembly geometry, total height, inner diameter, airtightness, laser joints, and downstream performance.
Development, cell engineering, process engineering, quality, production, purchasing, and related managers reviewed the lot results, internal quality/safety evidence, cell-performance evaluation, and official UN38.3 report. Based on that review, follow-on pilot production and purchase orders moved to the alternative can from March 2025. Existing inventory was consumed first, after which subsequent production input followed the new-can basis.
Standardization and handoff Change-review sheet: material, dimensional, and surface differences plus affected processes IQC criteria: measurement locations, dimensions, tolerances, burrs, and appearance disposition Part specification and limit samples: incoming component and surface criteria Process-condition sheet: beading, crimping/sizing, and can-cap laser conditions Sample-evaluation sheet: lot-level process, quality, safety, and performance results Supplier-approval package: official UN38.3 and cross-functional review results Purchasing and production handoff: criteria for pilot production and order change I prepared the change-risk logic, sample builds and evaluation, and the first drafts of the control documents. Quality, cell engineering, production, and purchasing reviewed the results so the same basis could be used from incoming inspection through production input.
Final results Established incoming and process-impact criteria for an alternative can with different alloy, thickness, tolerance, burr, and surface characteristics Reset applicable conditions on the existing beading, crimping/sizing, and can-cap laser equipment Connected internal sealing, compression, drop, and vent tests with formation, capacity, and life evaluation Completed a 600-cell pilot validation across three lots of 200 cells Passed the official UN38.3 transport-safety test Transitioned pilot production and purchase orders in March 2025 and handed off the field standards Related projects 2170 assembly-line good-yield stabilization: stabilized the process and inspection basis of the line receiving the alternative component 25P LFP Power Cell NPI process development, trial production, and customer qualification: connected material and component changes to cell CTQs and staged development validation

contents:
Project background and problem definition During early NCM pilot production, ultrasonic pre-welding repeatedly produced positive-electrode uncoated-edge tearing, active-material shedding around the negative heavy edge, and shorts. Reducing the welding condition lowered damage but also weakened the required joint. Manual pre-forming showed a workable direction, but position, pressure, and R geometry changed by operator.
Process decision: I rejected a condition compromise that traded joint strength for lower damage. The selected direction retained the pre-welding requirement, separated the damage mechanism by electrode, and controlled forming position and geometry through a pilot jig.
My direct scope covered damage reproduction and teardown analysis, positive/negative cause separation, pilot-jig concept and drawing, R geometry and forming-position definition, sample builds and inspection, process documents, training, and the production-equipment RFQ.
MECHANISM · JIG · LOT VALIDATIONResolve the damage without weakening the welding conditionEvidence: teardown, Short, Hi-Pot, IR, weld tensile, formation, and four lots01SIGNALTear, shedding, and short02TRADE-OFFLower damage versus joint strength03SEPARATEPositive Al foil and negative heavy edge04DESIGNR geometry, position, and stopper05VERIFYAbout 200 plus 4 lots×5006TRANSFERSOP, QCP, P-FMEA, and RFQ4M cause analysis and environment check Analysis target Suspected cause Finding Action Man Manual variation in forming position, pressure, and correct insertion Trained operators still showed about 1.5 mm of position variation and different damage results · Core variation source Convert insertion position and work sequence into jig criteria Machine No dedicated jig, forming tool, or position datum Damage changed with pre-forming condition under the same welding condition · Core manufacturing constraint Design electrode-specific pilot jigs, datum, and stopper Material Positive Al-foil tearing and negative heavy-edge active-material shedding Teardown showed different damage locations and forms by electrode · Material-specific separation Define electrode-specific R geometry and forming position Method Undefined forming direction, position, R geometry, and sequence Manual geometry was compared with shorts and teardown results · Core cause Establish forming, insertion, acceptance, and hold criteria Measurement and environment checks
Measurement: Appearance alone could not reveal internal damage or functional impact · Short, Hi-Pot, IR, tensile, formation, and teardown were cross-checked · Final decision basis · Connect electrical, weld, teardown, and cell evaluation in one flow Environment: Process-environment change · No repeated relationship with damage location or form · Removed as primary cause · Retain existing environmental controls Core process engineering 1. Separate the electrode-specific damage mechanisms I did not treat positive- and negative-electrode failures as one forming problem. Teardown location and damage geometry were used to define separate process criteria.
Area Observed failure mode Process-design decision Positive electrode Al-foil uncoated-edge tear and fracture Positive-specific R geometry and a gentler forming position Negative electrode Active-material shedding and excessive compression around the heavy edge Negative-specific R geometry and compression-limiting position Common acceptance Short and weld-quality risk One completion basis linking Short, Hi-Pot, IR, weld appearance/tensile, and teardown The weaker-welding alternative was rejected because tensile performance fell together with damage. Forming through the ultrasonic-welder motion was also rejected due to higher takt and added J/R damage risk. Pre-forming was therefore separated as its own operation.
2. Design the pilot jig and control operator variation One manually formed batch confirmed the damage-reduction direction. The next step converted position, pressure, and insertion variation into mechanical and work criteria.
Field variation Pilot-jig and work response Verification Operator forming-position variation Datum, stopper, and correct-insertion position Position, appearance, short, and teardown Direction and pressure differences Electrode-specific R geometry, insertion direction, and work sequence Coated-area compression and foil tearing Incorrect J/R insertion Correct-insertion and hold criteria Retraining and retest for a new operator Appearance blind spot Linked electrical, weld, teardown, and cell evaluation Hi-Pot, IR, tensile, formation, and life I prepared the pilot-jig concept and drawing and defined the positive/negative R geometry, forming position, and correct-insertion criteria. When incorrect insertion by a new operator reproduced the same damage, jig setting and insertion sequence were retrained and retested on the same basis.
3. Validate pilot processability across about 400 samples Action and retest Exploratory trials for narrowing geometry were separated from lot-level confirmation of the selected condition.

Appearance and correct insertion → Short, Hi-Pot, and IR → pre-weld appearance, tensile, and fracture mode → uncoated-edge and coated-area teardown → formation, capacity, cycling, and life Result and standardization The selected condition was confirmed on the same inspection basis across operator and lot changes. Project stageProduction readiness and limited-production setupPeriodFeb–Sep 2025RoleLead engineering ownerCore responsibilityThree laser processes and inspection/measurement standardsValidation scope100 cells × 2 lotsFinal result50-cell continuous run and limited-production approvalProject background and objective Product development and equipment SAT had been completed, but the actual new product did not match the inherited machine and inspection conditions. The line could not run continuously from Start to the final operation, and operators relied on unit-by-unit manual operation and temporary recipes, creating variation in welding, inspection, and final geometry.
Changes in product geometry, reflectivity, and turn count were also missing from the laser, AI-vision, and X-ray settings. After the previous development owners left, the engineering team re-established equipment geometry and process conditions using actual cells and separated setting-related problems from equipment that required mechanical or software changes.
The objective was to restore geometry and process conditions on three laser-welding machines, rebuild X-ray and AI-vision inspection reliability, and establish controlled manual work and inspection standards for equipment that could not be redesigned immediately. This created a practical limited-production setup capable of a continuous full-process run.
Equipment inspection findings Area Finding Direction Three laser-welding processes Temporary weld conditions had been built around poor jig contact, reference position, and alignment Restore machine geometry before optimizing weld conditions AI vision YOLO models trained on the original SAT product did not match the new geometry and reflectivity Separate reliable automatic inspection from visual inspection X-ray Original Count and ROI settings remained despite changes in turn count and internal geometry Reset automatic inspection through teardown and cross-section correlation Ready and sequence Operators reset product sensing, axis Home, and Ready conditions individually Rebuild automatic-ready conditions while retaining safety interlocks Filling, crimping, and marking Seal design, load transfer, and software editing had structural constraints Standardize temporary work and full inspection; transfer permanent actions through punch items Equipment inspection sequence Reviewed manual steps, recurring alarms, and product abnormalities with manufacturing operators. Restated each machine’s process function and the product characteristic it had to control. Restored jig contact, product reference position, alignment, and machine geometry on the laser equipment. Reset welding and inspection conditions only after the machines repeated their intended motion at the correct position. Correlated sectioning, tensile tests, cell teardown, X-ray, and AI-vision results through the same product flow. Separated adjustments that could be completed through settings from mechanical and software changes requiring redesign. Retested the complete process with two 100-cell lots and then ran a final 50 cells continuously from the first to the last operation. The correlated results were used to reset automatic inspection for turn count, electrode overlap, and overhang.

Once product sensor permissives and axis-position conditions were satisfied, the machine entered the automatic-ready state. Manufacturing trials confirmed that trained operators could prepare the equipment through one consistent sequence.
Measurement and inspection standardization I directly wrote or revised the criteria for joined layers, effective weld area, penetration depth, fracture form, AI-vision illumination/focus/inspection regions, the quality measurement standard, P-FMEA, and reference-sample management.
Vision setting sheets, limit samples, X-ray Count/ROI, manufacturing check sheets, QCP, manual MES entry, and visual-inspection training materials prepared by the engineering team were reviewed against the actual production conditions and aligned across departments.
Equipment design and software gaps with production controls Machines that could not be resolved through setting or recipe changes were separated into production controls and permanent improvement actions. Temporary work was standardized to protect production, while mechanical and software changes were transferred through punch lists and RFQ actions.
E/L Filling E/L Filling meters electrolyte into the cell and maintains the seal during filling. Leakage, insufficient and variable fill quantity, and contamination repeatedly occurred at the O-ring connection between the hopper and chamber.
Leakage and fill-variation disposition Analysis target Suspected cause Finding Action Man Spare replacement and leak/fill checks depended on operator judgment Compared replacement and inspection order by operator · Recurrence-control factor Standardize replacement, leakage, fill, and contamination checks Machine Hopper-to-chamber seal-joint design and O-ring dimensions Matched repeat leakage with seal-joint structure · Redesign item Use the existing spare for limited production and transfer redesign Material O-ring chemical-resistance requirement Compared supplier specification and chemical-response results with the requirement · Change requirement Reflect in material and dimensional requirements Method Spare replacement and checks for leakage, fill quantity, and seal contamination Compared production results before and after replacement · Temporary production condition Apply as limited-production standard work Measurement and environment checks

Supplier dimensions and chemical-reaction results were used to transfer a combined O-ring material/dimension and hopper-to-chamber joint change through the punch list and RFQ.
Crimping & Sizing Crimping & Sizing mechanically seals the can and cap and establishes final cell height and geometry. One press did not consistently reach the target height, requiring two to three repetitions and causing height variation, crimp-shape defects, can/cap deformation, 3-jaw sticking, and cycle stops.

Measurement: Pressure-sensitive sheets, height, inner diameter, appearance, sealing, leakage, drop, impact, and vent · Cross-checked product results with structural abnormalities · Limited-production evidence · Apply product-by-product disposition Grease quantity and motion speed were adjusted, and repeated pressing, product removal/reinsertion, and full inspection were standardized. Drive-system, load-transfer-center, and 3-jaw changes were transferred as permanent improvement actions.
Marking Marking applies lot, QR, and date information to the product and connects it with MES traceability. The original program fixed the format and did not allow a new QR pattern to be registered or an operator template to be changed.

Measurement: Visual inspection and scanner reading · Checked appearance and readability immediately after marking · Limited-production evidence · Apply visual and scanner criteria Operators entered the lot and QR data, ran marking, checked the result visually and with a scanner, and recorded it in MES under one standard procedure. New-pattern registration, input templates, and user-editing functions were transferred as software improvement actions.
Washing retained its existing conditions because no representative issue blocked the production transition.
Production validation and limited-production approval Preliminary retest: Two 100-cell lots were run through the complete 4695 assembly process to revalidate equipment motion, welding/inspection results, and process-to-process connections. Final continuous run: A final 50 cells were produced continuously from the first to the last operation under a defined combination of automatic and manual work. Operating conditions: V3/V4 automatic inspection; V1/V2/V5 visual inspection and MES entry; filling leak/fill checks; repeated crimping; and manual marking were managed as standard work. Based on the validation results and work standards, I submitted the technical recommendation for the limited-production range. Development, quality, manufacturing, and manufacturing-innovation managers approved the scope, completing the production-readiness handoff.
Standardization and handoff Work standards, QCP, and P-FMEA Manufacturing check sheets and quality measurement standards Equipment punch lists, reference samples, and limit samples MES key-control items and manual-entry procedures Visual-inspection and operator-training materials E/L Filling spare-parts list, modification request, and RFQ I prepared the first drafts and aligned the field-use scope with engineering, maintenance, manufacturing, and quality. Production checks and manual work were separated from permanent improvement actions so the next owners could operate and continue the redesign under the same basis.

Two 100-cell lots and the final 50-cell continuous full-process run validated the limited-production setup, followed by management approval and handoff of the field standards.

30-second summary
Before trying to improve the yield number, I separated inspection errors from actual process defects so that equipment and process actions targeted the right cause.Production stabilization resultPeriod / basisDuring tenure at Kumyang · May 2024–Sep 2025Project formCompany project · Assembly process leadProblem to solveEffective good yield was initially about 40%, while production, quality, and equipment teams were using different denominators and defect definitions.
My scopeAligned production, inspection, retest, scrap, and defect definitions, then coordinated improvement schedules and retest results.Used MSA results to separate judgement errors from real defects, then checked jig tolerance, recipe, consumables, vision, and inspection conditions one factor at a time.Verified result / current stageMeasured result · TeamEffective good yield in the reviewed scope: about 40%→98.7%Verified output · IndividualReflected confirmed conditions in SOP, QCP, P-FMEA, inspection criteria, and training materialTeam boundaryYield was a cross-functional team result. My role as assembly process lead was to align criteria, priorities, and revalidation.
Disclosure scope: Company source data and customer specifications are confidential, so this case is anonymized and limited to career records and work I directly performed.
The sequence below generalizes the actual work within a publicly shareable scope.
The three-minute case Why it mattered Good-product yield on the 2170 assembly line was initially about 40%. Changing equipment conditions from that headline number alone could mistake a judgment error for a real defect. The reverse was equally risky: treating an actual process defect as an inspection issue would allow it to recur. Before changing the process, the production, inspection, retest, and scrap quantities needed one yield denominator.
My scope As the assembly-process lead, I organized the production plan, WIP, defects, and downtime. I aligned the denominator and defect names used by production, quality, equipment, and development, coordinated the MSA review and condition-by-condition retests, and carried confirmed conditions into field standards.
Workflow Align the yield denominator → separate judgment error from actual defects with MSA → check jigs, recipes, consumables, and inspection conditions → retest one condition at a time → update SOP, QCP, and P-FMEA
Key decisions and verification I used MSA to review operator judgment error and measurement-system variation before classifying actual process defects. Jigs, recipes, consumable wear, and inspection conditions were checked as one system, but only one condition changed in each trial. The test item, inspection method, and decision rule stayed fixed. A condition entered the line baseline only after repeat results supported it. Result and standardization The team result recorded in career material was an improvement in good-product yield from about 40% to 98.7%. Confirmed conditions and checks were added to SOPs, QCP, P-FMEA, inspection criteria, and operator training. The practical standard was that different operators and shifts would calculate and judge yield on the same basis.
Transferability When yield is low, verify the denominator and the measurement system before tuning a recipe. Then separate equipment, consumable, and inspection variables and retest one condition at a time so the cause and effect remain explainable.
Limits The 98.7% figure is a career result for this line, verification period, and denominator, not a public-data recalculation or a universal result for every 2170 line. Company drawings, recipes, raw quality records, and customer specifications remain confidential.
Links and evidence Public linksPublic material for reviewing project evidence and the live user surface.
There is no separate public GitHub repository or report. Quantitative results are described from career records.
In an interview I can explain how the denominator was aligned, how MSA separated judgment error, the sequence of retests, and the scope of the standard-work updates.

GoalSeparate signal quality, equipment state, process conditions, and measurement behavior, then lock validated conditions into standards, QCP, P-FMEA, and MSA.
SuccessStabilize verified-scope 2170 good-product yield from about 40% to 98.7% and record accepted conditions in SOP, QCP, P-FMEA, and inspection criteria.

The article generalizes how ontology and wiki knowledge is selected to compose and run an agent through a practical work example.
What this platform is Approval gates are not the product by themselves. This project is an AI agent platform that uses knowledge, terminology, and operating rules from an ontology and an LLM wiki to compose and run an agent for a requested task.
The ontology connects related concepts such as equipment, processes, documents, and roles. The LLM wiki provides task guidance, operating sequences, tool instructions, and cautions. The platform selects the relevant knowledge and assembles an executable agent definition containing its role, tools, evidence sources, output format, and stop conditions.
Authority, approval, and evidence checks are the platform’s safety layer. The ability to generate an answer does not automatically permit an agent to submit an order, deploy a change, or modify access. Evidence and human approval are checked separately before an external effect is allowed.
Why I built it When an agent is defined only through a long prompt, terminology can be interpreted inconsistently and the same rules must be repeated for every project. Source documents and tool boundaries also become mixed into the conversation. As the number of agents grows, knowledge and operating rules are duplicated, and a correction may reach only some agents.
I separated reusable knowledge into the ontology and wiki, then selected only the parts needed for each execution. The goal was to make an agent’s knowledge and action boundary inspectable outside its prompt and let several agents share the same knowledge contract.
Representative user scene Consider a request to identify likely causes of repeated equipment stops and propose an inspection sequence.
Classify the equipment, symptom, related process, and expected output in the request. Find connected equipment, parts, failure modes, and inspection documents in the ontology. Retrieve the sequence, allowed tools, sources, and restrictions from the LLM wiki. Compose the analysis agent’s role, inputs, tools, output format, and stop conditions. Run the agent within the allowed data and tool boundary while recording its evidence and result. If the task would change an external system, check the human approval scope, allow or stop the action, and read back the actual result after execution. This is a generalized public description of the implemented direction. It excludes company documents, equipment addresses, accounts, and private operating rules.
A system map for first-time readers This platform is not a single chatbot screen. It has an entry point for the request, an ontology and wiki that supply relevant knowledge, a composition stage that assembles a task-specific agent, a bounded execution stage, and a final evidence and result check.
Five stages of the AI agent platformThe ontology and LLM wiki supply the agent's knowledge and operating rules. Authority and evidence checks remain separate before and after execution. Because there is no public operating UI at this stage, this diagram shows the relationship among the locally validated components.
Generalized from the locally validated foundation·31 Jul 2026
A first-time reader can follow the diagram from left to right. The first three stages decide what agent should be composed. The last two decide what that agent may actually do and whether the observed result matches the request. Answer quality and permission to change an external system therefore remain separate concerns.
Components and responsibilities Component Responsibility Ontology Connect domain concepts and relationships so agents resolve the same objects consistently LLM wiki Provide task guidance, tool instructions, examples, constraints, and validation criteria Agent Composer Turn a request into an executable definition of role, tools, evidence, output, and stop conditions Agent Runner Execute the definition within its allowed boundary and record the process and result Authority & Evidence Layer Check evidence, target identity, and human approval; stop when information is missing and read back the result after execution This separation means a knowledge change can be made in the ontology or wiki instead of editing every agent prompt. The runner records which knowledge was used, while the safety layer keeps analytical success separate from execution authority.
Source structure and reading order The actual repository is not public. The names below are generalized responsibility units for explaining the codebase; they are not copies of private directory names.
knowledge/ ├── ontology/ relationships among equipment, process, documents, and roles └── wiki/ task sequences, tool guidance, and cautions schemas/ agent execution and evidence contracts composer/ selects knowledge and assembles an agent definition runner/ invokes permitted tools and records the run authority/ checks target, human approval, and external-effect scope evidence/ preserves sources, artifact identity, and observed results tests/ exercises stop conditions, replay, and artifact consistency For a first code read, start with knowledge/ to see what an agent can know. Continue through schemas/ and composer/ to see how that knowledge becomes an executable definition. Then read runner/ and authority/ for the action boundary, followed by evidence/ and tests/ for result verification.
Data, AI, and human roles The ontology and wiki retain concepts, relationships, task guidance, sources, scope, and constraints. An agent run records the request, selected knowledge, tools, result, risk, and approval boundary separately. This makes it possible to inspect how an agent was composed and which material it used.
AI assists with request classification, candidate knowledge retrieval, agent-definition drafts, test and counterexample creation, and result summaries. A person reviews the ontology and wiki, chooses the permitted tools and data scope, and approves any external change. A better answer does not transfer human authority to the agent.

It does not mean that a public service, live trading, or external-system automation is operational.

Knowledge remains in the ontology and wiki, while each agent receives only the role and tools required for its task, reducing duplicated knowledge and prompt variation.
The platform can also retain which knowledge and documents were used, who approved an external change, and what the external system reported afterward. Actual benefit would still need to be measured through company-data integration, user validation, and operating-environment tests.

Real operation still requires quality review of the company ontology and wiki, document-level access control, bounded agent tools, human approval, duplicate-execution protection, and read-back from the external system. Why the shop-floor decision mattered Deep-learning code can run once and still be unusable for an engineering decision if no one can explain which data and settings produced the result. A score can be overstated when samples from the same product or Lot cross training and test boundaries, or when the test set is repeatedly used to guide model changes.
In manufacturing, that problem affects quality decisions directly. Missed defects and false rejections have different costs, and offline behavior can change with equipment, material, or capture conditions. The project therefore starts with a traceable experiment standard rather than a peak score.
Why a digital method was needed A single notebook is useful for fast exploration, but hidden state and cell order can make a result fragile. Separating preprocessing, training, evaluation, and run records makes it possible to trace which change affected the outcome.
MLOps in this case does not mean that a deployment platform has already been built. It means connecting the data identifier, split rule, configuration, code, runtime environment, and evaluation output as one experiment record.
My actual role As a personal learning project, I organized preprocessing, model architecture, evaluation, and system design into topic-based documents, then connected them to a PyTorch training template and a manufacturing-defect example. The repository aims for a path from data splitting and preprocessing through training, evaluation, and reproducibility, but the current public code implements only part of that path as a learning scaffold.
It therefore does not claim a specific dataset size, model accuracy, reproduced training result, or production deployment. Model, industry-case, and performance statements in the study documents are kept separate from repository achievements unless a corresponding run is publicly evidenced.

What an interviewer should confirm in 30 seconds Item Scope Project form A 10-person training-team PoC, not a live GIGA Press installation Problem Reduce rework caused by first aligning sequences, interlocks, screen tags, and upper-layer data on physical equipment What I led Overall planning of the topic, problem, scope, architecture, and integration order; final-report writing Direct hands-on scope The Digital Twin–AI integration structure, including the AI insertion point and authority boundary Teammate implementation Detailed PLC Ladder/Factory I/O and SCADA/OPC UA implementation Verified output An integrated Factory I/O–PLC/Ladder–SCADA/OPC UA–web team demo and final report Not verified Physical GIGA Press behavior, safety PLC, HIL/FAT, production impact, or DQN closed-loop performance I was not the project manager or the sole developer. The team lead managed schedule, risk, and the final presentation. I led the overall structure and integration order, wrote the final report, and directly worked on the Digital Twin–AI connection. This distinction shows system-level judgement without attributing teammates’ Ladder and SCADA work to me.
How the problem was framed A GIGA Press can consolidate many body components and downstream assembly steps, but its scale and capital cost make repeated physical try-out expensive. The team therefore treated the assignment as a virtual-commissioning and interface problem.
The report framed repeated physical try-out, design/equipment data mismatch, and disconnected live state as the commissioning problems.This project did not model molten-metal filling, die thermal deformation, casting pressure, or other physical die-casting behavior. Factory I/O represented the GIGA Press stage with a simplified CNC process, followed by inspection, tray transfer, stacker loading, and release.
Material input → machining (CNC substitute) → good/defect decision → good tray transfer → stacker loading → release command → defect discharge Factory I/O simplified the scope to machining, inspection, transfer, stacking, and release rather than modelling die-casting physics.The precise question was therefore:
Not whether the project reproduced a full GIGA Press, but whether process sequence and cross-layer data responsibility could be reviewed before physical equipment arrived.

"recommendation" .-> BThe important design decision was not merely adding AI. It was defining who owns final machine authority.
Layer Responsibility Boundary Factory I/O Reproduce process motion and virtual sensor/actuator states Does not prove hydraulic, servo, die, or safety behavior PLC/Ladder Sequence, interlocks, stop/restart logic, and final run permission Does not execute network or AI output without validation SCADA Display state, alarms, and operator-command results Does not replace safety circuits or PLC interlocks OPC UA/Web Provide a readable upper-layer data path Successful communication does not prove data validity or safety AI candidate Evaluate optimization possibilities from equipment state Does not own emergency stop, safety judgement, or machine authority The training report uses language about DQN real-time learning and control. This public case deliberately limits that claim to DQN candidate selection and integration design. There was no repeated live-equipment dataset, validated response time, safety-constrained closed loop, or production comparison.
Decisions and deliverables I owned 1. Fixed the virtual-commissioning scope before discussing AI Claiming to reproduce the full physics of a GIGA Press within a short training project would create an unverifiable scope. I limited the scenario to machining–inspection–transfer–stacking and focused the team on the PLC, SCADA, OPC UA, web, and AI interfaces that could actually be demonstrated.
2. Connected separate team implementations through one integration order The overall plan followed this sequence:
Define normal flow and stop conditions in Factory I/O. Make the PLC own step transitions and interlocks. Show the same state and alarms from the operator’s SCADA perspective. Define the upper-layer data boundary through OPC UA. Allow web and AI consumers to read the data without taking PLC authority. Teammates implemented the detailed Ladder/Factory I/O and SCADA/OPC UA components. My contribution was to define how those outputs fit one process meaning and sequence, then integrate the team result in the final report.
3. Defined the Digital Twin–AI insertion point I did not begin with the statement that AI would autonomously control the line. I first separated:
which virtual-sensor and PLC states could become AI inputs; what recommendation, rather than direct machine command, could be returned; how the recommendation would remain below PLC interlocks and run permission; how stale data, network loss, and reconnection would invalidate the recommendation. This established a DQN candidate location and data path. It did not prove model superiority or field performance.
4. Separated verified output from expected benefit in the final report The team material includes expected statements such as a 50–75% setup-time reduction, 50% lower expansion effort, minimized MTTR, and zero hardware-damage risk. These were not measured through a live-factory before/after comparison and are not presented as my achievements.
Category Public wording Verified team output Integrated virtual process, PLC, SCADA, OPC UA, web demo, and report Verified individual contribution Overall planning, final report, and Digital Twin–AI integration structure Expected benefit / next stage Possible virtual-commissioning time reduction, reusable modules, predictive-maintenance and energy-management extensions Team and individual boundaries Scope Attribution Problem definition, scope, architecture, and cross-team integration order Overall planning led by me Final-report structure and writing My direct deliverable Digital Twin data to AI-candidate insertion point and authority boundary My main hands-on scope Detailed PLC Ladder and Factory I/O implementation Teammates Detailed SCADA and OPC UA server/client implementation Teammates Schedule, risk management, and final presentation Team lead Factory I/O–PLC–SCADA–OPC UA–web integrated demonstration 10-person team output My interview description is therefore:
I led the project’s problem definition, scope, architecture, and integration order and wrote the final report. My direct technical scope was Digital Twin–AI integration. Teammates implemented the Ladder and SCADA layers, and the integrated demonstration was a 10-person team result.
Verified results The attached report contains result screens for:
Ladder linked to the Factory I/O virtual equipment; a SCADA view linked to stacker states and the virtual line; a web dashboard with equipment, alarm, and AI-analysis areas; a proposed PLC–OPC UA–Factory I/O–AI architecture. Team integration evidence across PLC/Factory I/O, SCADA/stacker supervision, and the web operating view. These screens do not establish live-factory performance.These screens support an integrated training demonstration across multiple layers. They do not support the following claims:
reproduction of live GIGA Press casting quality or dynamics; stable production control by DQN within 0.1 seconds; superiority or greater stability than PPO, MARL, or Transformer methods; measured setup-time reduction of 50–75% or expansion-effort reduction of 50%; deployed predictive-maintenance or energy-management models. Interview questions and answer boundaries Why use a Digital Twin? To review missing sensors, sequence delays, stops, restarts, and cross-layer signal mismatches before discovering them on physical equipment. The value of this PoC is the pre-commissioning logic and interface review process, not a high-fidelity physical model.
Why did AI not directly control the PLC? AI inference and networks contain latency and uncertainty, while the training model had no validated safety integrity. Final run permission and interlocks therefore remain in the PLC, with AI limited to an upper-layer recommendation candidate.
Why was DQN selected? Its state–action–value structure was suitable for explaining action candidates under different process states in a training setting. The project did not conclude that DQN was better than alternative reinforcement-learning methods. State, reward, safety constraints, and baselines require new comparison before field use.
What is the largest limitation? Factory I/O cannot replace live GIGA Press physics or its safety system. The project also lacks representative field data, long-duration communication testing, operator-alarm validation, and AI closed-loop testing.
Validation required before field use Hardware-in-the-Loop testing with real I/O and a safety PLC. Missing-sensor, stale-value, network-loss, reconnect, and restart scenarios. Quality and timestamp alignment for AI inputs and explicit recommendation invalidation. PLC interlocks, approve/reject/rollback procedures, and manual-operation priority. Before/after measures under the same basis: debugging time, tag mismatches, recovery time, and retest count. Stability under real takt, load, and long-duration operation. Disclosure scope Internal edit links and source material are not published. This case separates team output, individual contribution, expected effect, and unverified scope based on the attached report and the role boundaries confirmed by me. No external report button is displayed until a sanitized view-only report is available.

The integrated demo is a team result. DQN closed-loop performance and the 50–75%/50% reduction figures were not measured in a live factory. External report links remain withheld until a redacted view-only version is verified.

What this project is The same machine or defect can have different names across manufacturing documents. HeungTology is a personal experiment that stores industrial-knowledge documents as Markdown nodes and indexes their YAML front matter and body text in a local vector store. It is a Git repository containing a knowledge collection and a local Python CLI, not a public web service or graph dashboard.

On the shop floor, the cost of missing a defect can matter more than aggregate accuracy, so the PoC separated data sources and prioritized recall and threshold decisions.Detection-criteria evaluation stagePeriod / basisTraining team project · Public case updated Jul 2026Project formManufacturing DX PoC · Before production useProblem to solveA model that performs well on public data cannot be assumed to behave the same on field images with different lighting, angles, and surface conditions.
My scopeSeparated public training data from field practice images and ordered metric and threshold review around missed-defect risk.Verified result / current stageVerified output · IndividualPublic/field data separation and a recall- and threshold-led evaluation flowCurrent stage · TeamTraining PoC complete; not production-deployedTeam boundaryThis was a training-team PoC; model results are not presented as production-quality performance.
Disclosure scope: Field images and company quality criteria are not disclosed; only the data separation and decision process are described.
The path from data collection to possible production use is generalized to the publicly shareable PoC scope.
The first minute This case is a training-team Vision AI PoC that classifies weld images into normal and defect candidates. It was not a system that replaced inspectors or made shipment decisions. The team evaluated whether a model could narrow the images that an inspector should review first.
Item What to know Problem The risk of missing small weld defects when normal images dominate the data Team output Public/field data separation, staged model experiments, a second test, and a result report My scope Data-purpose separation, metric and comparison design, and recall-first threshold review Current stage Training PoC evaluation complete; not production-deployed Public screen No runnable inspection screen or report capture is available; only the shareable decision flow is explained The 30-second summary at the top shows the outcome and role boundary first. The main text explains why recall came first, how data moved through the PoC, and how the team result differs from my contribution. The expandable Design and validation record below is the supporting requirements and task appendix.
Why weld-defect detection matters A missed micro-crack or pinhole can allow a defective weld to continue downstream. Flagging a normal part as a defect candidate creates reinspection work. Both have a cost, but this project gave priority to reducing the error that passes a defect as normal.
When normal images greatly outnumber defect images, a model can report high accuracy by predicting normal most of the time. The evaluation therefore did not stop at “How many images were correct?” It considered recall—the share of actual defects found—together with precision, which helps describe the reinspection load.
My battery-cell assembly experience with ultrasonic and laser welding informed that priority. The field experience and the education-project metrics remain separate, however. This case evaluates inspection-assistance potential on bounded material; it does not claim completed autonomous inspection.
Complete system architecture flowchart LRA["AI-Hub public imagesabout 60,000"] --> C["Check label meaning,duplicates, and split"]B["Field-practice images198"] --> D["Separate field-response check"]C --> E["Team model experimentsDenseNet → two-model → ResNet+DeiT"]E --> F["Defect probabilityfor each image"]F --> G["Search decision thresholds"]G --> H["Precision, recall, and F1Confusion matrix"]D --> I["Review FP and FN images"]H --> II --> J["Inspection-assistance rule"]J --> K["Inspector recheck"]K --> L["Next data andcapture-condition review"]This diagram summarizes the publicly shareable PoC flow. It does not mean that the team implemented an operating production system in which a line camera streamed images to a real-time model.
Component Responsibility Not established at this stage Public data Provide broad learning coverage for weld-defect features Prove field performance Field images Check model response under limited capture conditions Represent every machine and product condition Team model experiments Compare stages from DenseNet to ResNet+DeiT Select an operating model from model name alone Threshold evaluation Compare where a defect probability becomes a review candidate Fix one value for every future condition Inspection-assistance rule Send higher-risk candidates to human reinspection Make shipment decisions without a person Error review Return FP and FN cases to data and capture review Assume every error has one model-only cause How data, models, and evaluation connect 1. Separate the purpose of each data source Approximately 60,000 AI-Hub public welding images supplied broad learning coverage. 198 field-practice images provided a separate, limited check under field capture conditions. The two sources were not presented as one undifferentiated set of 60,198 training images. Cameras, illumination, surface reflections, and product conditions differed. Strong results on public data were not treated as proof of the same behavior in the field.
2. Check labels and splits The workflow aligned the meaning of public labels with the field defect definition and kept the same image from appearing in both learning and evaluation. If that boundary fails, a high score may only show that the model saw the same image again.
3. Compare the team’s model stages on one basis The team experiment record progressed from a DenseNet-stage baseline through a two-model combination to a ResNet+DeiT ensemble. The stages were compared under the same F1, recall, and precision frame instead of changing the success rule for each model. I do not present all of that model development as solo work.
4. Turn probabilities into an inspection rule The model outputs a defect probability for each image. A threshold decides when that probability becomes a defect candidate. Lowering the threshold can catch more defects, but it can also send more normal images to reinspection.
Term Plain meaning Why it mattered here Recall The share of actual defects the model found Reduce missed defects first Precision The share of defect candidates that were actual defects Understand the reinspection load F1 A balance between recall and precision Avoid choosing from one favorable metric False negative A defect predicted as normal The error reduced first False positive A normal image predicted as a defect candidate The error connected to reinspection cost 5. Look back at the images behind the metrics The second test reviewed the region where normal and defect predictions mixed. The evaluation first found thresholds that retained 100% recall, compared precision and F1 within that region, and then reviewed FP and FN images to identify the next questions for data, labels, and capture conditions.
Team result versus my contribution Scope Attribution Public and field data preparation, model training and candidate progression, second test, and PoC report Training-team result Separating the intended use of public data and field images My role Organizing a common F1, recall, and precision comparison My role Reviewing recall-first thresholds and interpreting FP and FN behavior My role A claim that I built every model alone, a real-time inspection screen, or production deployment Not claimed as my work In an interview, I explain the complete flow and the work I actually performed. This keeps the team’s models and report as team output while making my evaluation and operating-threshold contribution concrete.
Problems and decisions Problem Decision Reason Normal images can make accuracy hide missed-defect risk Use recall first and inspect precision and F1 with it Separate defect-pass risk from reinspection cost Public and field images have different capture conditions Keep their purposes separate Avoid presenting public-data results as field performance One model behaves differently at different thresholds Compare precision and F1 inside the 100%-recall region Evaluate model choice and inspection policy together Metrics alone do not reveal why errors happened Review the confusion matrix and FP/FN images Return findings to data, label, and capture review Field material and the report cannot be published as-is Publish only a verified text structure Avoid fabricated screens or images with unclear rights Verified result and potential benefits At the selected threshold on the recorded evaluation set, the report lists F1 93.10%, Recall 100%, and Precision 87.07%. Recall 100% means that no defect in that evaluation set was missed. It does not guarantee every future defect or every equipment condition. Precision 87.07% shows that some defect candidates may be normal and require reinspection.
The benefit demonstrated by the PoC was not one metric in isolation. It was a way to turn quality risk into an inspection policy:
a review priority that puts higher-cost candidates in front of an inspector first; one evaluation frame for comparing model candidates; a shared language that links missed defects to quality risk and false alarms to reinspection; and a sequence for returning recurring error images to data and capture improvement. A reduction in escaped defects or inspection time was not measured. Such effects require a controlled comparison before and after production introduction.
Current limitations and next validation The current stage is a bounded PoC. The 198 field images do not cover every equipment, material, lighting, and product-shape condition. Real-time camera input, inference at line speed, dropped frames, long-term performance change, and the operator reinspection procedure were not validated.
Field use would require the following checks:
Build an independent evaluation set split by product or lot. Reconfirm class-level sample counts and label rules with quality specialists. Standardize camera position, illumination, focus, and capture timing. Test inference latency and dropped frames at line speed. Trace model version, threshold, image, equipment condition, and reinspection result together. Provide change approval and a path back to an earlier model and threshold. Public-source and screen boundary There is currently no verified dedicated model-code repository, runnable inspection screen, or view-only report for this case. Field images and company quality criteria are also not disclosed. The page therefore does not substitute another project’s screen or a third-party welding image.
